newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN sees most Serbs staying for Croatian rule.
newsitem.headline: UN sees most Serbs staying for Croatian rule.

text.p: Most Serbs in Croatia's last separatist enclave will probably swallow hard and stay for the return of central government rule but their interests are being hurt by myopic local leaders, U.N. authorities say.

Eastern Slavonia, a fertile Danube valley plain, is due to be reintegrated in Croatia soon after April elections in a peaceful end to six years of ethnic conflict punctuated by the government's reconquest of two other Serb enclaves.
Fear of vengeful violence by refugees in the pre-1991 Croat majority community who will reclaim their homes under reintegration haunts the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia.

But there is also cautious hope stirred by a Croatian pledge of major minority rights, made after arduous U.N. mediation, which U.N. officials believe has helped discredit Serb extremists and will encourage most Serbs not to flee.

Jacques Klein, the American diplomat who heads the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), said the best "guesstimate" was that between 15,000 and 20,000 of the 120,000-odd Serbs would be sure to leave for nearby Serbia.

"These are Serb nationalists who simply cannot live in a Croatian Catholic state, and they include war criminals, people with guilty consciences," Klein said in an interview at his compound in Vukovar, the enclave's war-devastated main city.

Minority Serbs seized Eastern Slavonia in a 1991 uprising against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia that was scarred by atrocities including the demolition of Vukovar in a marathon Serb siege and the massacre of 260 Croat hospital patients.

UNTAES spokesman Philip Arnold said only about 650 Serb households left Eastern Slavonia from June 1996, when rebel forces withdrew under U.N. supervision, to January 1997, but 450 had gone in the first 10 days of February alone.

He said the radical increase in departures followed a U.N. Security Council decision on January 29 relegating Serb demands for a single administrative district -- a last-gasp bid to preserve autonomy unacceptable to Zagreb -- "in the coffin".
But more than 40,000 Serbs have meanwhile obtained Croatian citizenship papers in order to vote, keep their property and jobs and qualify for pensions and other social benefits.

Klein, a vigorous "can-do" American who has sought to instil the idea of positive thinking in a culture crippled by obsessions with the past, feels Serbs will have a fair shake in Croatia if only they take advantage of their opportunities.
The Croatian government, in a Letter of Intent to the Security Council, has pledged a host of Serb rights unheard of in this highly centralised and nationalist republic.
Serbs were promised the posts of assistant minister in the republic ministries of reconstruction, interior, justice and education and senior positions in the Office of Refugees.
They would also get the posts of deputy administrator in the two counties comprising the enclave and proportional representation in the region's police force and judiciary.
Provisions for cultural and education autonomy would include Serb schools and radio stations, Klein said.
But Serb leaders have tended to dismiss the package as insincere, a ploy to lull international observers while discrimination and score-settling go on behind the scenes.

"It is only a fiction that people chosen for these minority posts will be able to accomplish anything as Serbs," said Vojin Susa, the Serbs' envoy for legal issues who like other Serb leaders thinks more than half their people will flee.

"What counts is the high degree of animosity between ordinary Croats and Serbs. The methods and short timetable for reintegration are just another tragi-comic effort of the international community in former Yugoslavia."

Klein said Serb leaders, instead of appreciating Western pressure on Croatia to keep its promises on pain of losing foreign investment, were wallowing in an ancient martyr complex that prefers heroic defeat to success achieved by compromise.
He said Serb leaders had dwelled during meetings with Croatian envoys on impossible demands for autonomy instead of taking the Croats up on offers of various rights and posts.

"They have this irrational, almost theological (agenda), as if the angel Gabriel will come back. We urge them to guarantee themselves protection by being inside the system and looking out, instead of outside looking in," Klein said.
